pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–10y; multiply up to 4-digit × 1-digit AND 2-digit × 2-digit using formal long multiplication, illustrated with the area model.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.5 — 'fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm'; 4.NBT.5 covers up to 4-digit × 1-digit with area/place-value strategies.
• Operational details — the new challenge over Y4 short multiplication is the TWO-DIGIT multiplier: 34×27 requires multiplying by both the ones (7) and the tens (20), then adding partial products. The area model (45×23 as four sub-rectangles 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3) is the conceptual scaffold that shows WHY there are two rows of partial products and why the second row is shifted (it's ×20, not ×2). The classic error — forgetting the placeholder zero on the second partial product — is precisely a lost-place-value error the area model prevents. Estimate first (34×27≈30×30=900) to bound the answer.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): 4-digit × 1-digit (2347×6) securely. Tier B (age 9–10): 2-digit × 2-digit long multiplication (34×27) with correct partial-product placement. Tier C (age 10): draw the matching area model and explain why the second partial product is shifted / carries a zero.
bestPractices: Anchor long multiplication in the area model: 2-digit×2-digit as four sub-rectangles, so the two partial-product rows and the shift are seen as ×ones and ×tens.
Make the placeholder zero meaningful — the second row is ×20 (tens), not ×2 — rather than a rule to 'put a zero down'.
Estimate first by rounding both factors to bound the answer and catch magnitude errors.
Progress grid method → expanded partial products → compact long multiplication, keeping the area link visible.
Check with the inverse or by comparing to the estimate; watch carrying across multiple columns.
keyRepresentations: Area/grid model with four sub-rectangles (the home of the partial products)
Expanded partial-products layout bridging grid to compact form
Compact long-multiplication layout with the placeholder zero
Estimation (rounding both factors) to bound the product
commonMisconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the second partial product (treating ×20 as ×2).
Multiplying only by the ones digit of the two-digit multiplier and forgetting the tens.
Carrying errors across several columns, or adding carries into the wrong place.
Misaligning partial products when adding them.
Not connecting the algorithm to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.

learn.summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning formal long multiplication (up to 4-digit × 1-digit and 2-digit × 2-digit), anchor the written algorithm in the area model so the two partial-product rows and the placeholder zero become meaningful place-value facts rather than memorised rules. The central objective: the child sees that the second partial-product row is '×20 (tens)', not '×2', and that the four sub-rectangles of an area model sum to the same total as the two added partial products. Estimation by rounding both factors bounds the answer and catches magnitude slips.

activities.title: Bridge the area model to the written method (34 × 27)
feedback: If the second partial product comes out as 68 instead of 680: you multiplied by 2 instead of 20. Look at the 34×20 region of your grid — it is twenty rows worth 680, not 68. Write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.

If you only computed 34 × 7 and stopped: every part of 27 (both the 20 and the 7) must multiply every part of 34. Check your grid has all four regions — a missing region means a missing partial product.
If you wrote 34×2 + 34×7: you split 27 into digits 2 and 7 without place value. The tens digit is worth 20, so draw the ×20 regions explicitly.
If 238 + 680 doesn't total 918, recheck your column alignment and any carries — your estimate of ~900 tells you the answer should be near there.
activities.rationale: Coupling a partitioned area model to the columnar layout makes the place value of each partial product (and the meaning of the placeholder zero) visible, so a lost place value can be self-diagnosed. A live split-screen where partitioning tiles fill the long-multiplication frame, with tiles sliding together to show 600+210+80+28 = 918 matching the two added partials, is one concrete way to make this mechanism visible; a running estimate panel can flag magnitude slips.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Estimate first by rounding both factors: 34 × 27 ≈ 30 × 30 = 900, and keep this estimate in view as you work.
Draw an area model for 34 × 27 and partition it into four labelled sub-rectangles: 30×20, 30×7, 4×20, 4×7.
Alongside, set up the long-multiplication layout and compute the first partial product 34 × 7 = 238 (which is the 30×7 and 4×7 tiles: 210 + 28).
Compute the second partial product 34 × 20 = 680, writing a 0 in the ones place FIRST because this whole row is ×20, i.e. tens (this is the 30×20 and 4×20 tiles: 600 + 80).
Add the two partial products: 238 + 680 = 918, and confirm it matches the sum of all four area tiles (600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918).
Check the result against your estimate of 900 — are they close?
activities.intendedInsight: The second partial-product row is shifted and carries a placeholder zero because it is ×20 (tens), not ×2; the four area sub-rectangles are exactly the same quantities as the two written partial products broken apart, so the algorithm and the area model are two views of the same calculation.

activities.title: Secure 4-digit × 1-digit short multiplication (2,347 × 6)
feedback: If a carry is added into the wrong column, recheck each step and compare with your estimate. Note that rounding 2,347 DOWN (to 2,000 or 2,300) gives an underestimate, so the true answer should sit a little above those figures — 14,082 (just over 13,800) is reasonable.
If any column is skipped, remember every digit of 2,347 must be multiplied by 6.
activities.rationale: This activity enacts the Y5 curriculum requirement to multiply a number up to four digits by a one-digit number using a formal written method; it also secures the carrying and place-value fluency that two-digit long multiplication builds on, forming a sensible progression before the two-row layout.
sourceClaims: Y5 pupils multiply numbers up to 4 digits by a one- or two-digit number using a formal written method, including long multiplication for two-digit numbers.
learnerActions: Estimate first: 2,347 × 6 ≈ 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 (or 2,300 × 6 = 13,800 for a tighter bound).
Compute 2,347 × 6 in formal written layout, carrying across each column: 7×6=42 (write 2 carry 4), 4×6=24 plus 4 = 28 (write 8 carry 2), 3×6=18 plus 2 = 20 (write 0 carry 2), 2×6=12 plus 2 = 14.
Read off the answer 14,082 and check it against your estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit requires multiplying every digit and correctly handling carries across several columns; estimation bounds the magnitude.

activities.title: Map each written partial product to its area region (45 × 23)
feedback: If a region is missing or a partial product doesn't account for the full value of a digit, redraw the grid so every part of 23 (20 and 3) multiplies every part of 45 (40 and 5).
If the ×20 partial product lacks its placeholder zero, link it to the 800 + 100 = 900 tens regions: the row lives in the tens.
If the two totals (region sum and partial-product sum) disagree, recheck each region's arithmetic against the matching partial.
activities.rationale: Explicitly connecting the four area regions to the two partial products is the discriminating task that separates understanding from rote execution, and it directly targets the common error of omitting partial products.
sourceClaims: The area model should scaffold long multiplication, making partial products and the placeholder zero (× tens) meaningful.
learnerActions: Draw an area model for 45 × 23 with four regions: 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3.
Add all four regions to get the product: 800 + 120 + 100 + 15 = 1,035.
Now compute 45 × 23 by long multiplication and point to which area regions make up each partial product: 45×3 = 135 (= 120 + 15) and 45×20 = 900 (= 800 + 100).
Confirm the two partial products 135 + 900 = 1,035 equal the sum of the four area regions.
activities.intendedInsight: Each written partial product is a sum of two area sub-rectangles, so a child who can map regions to partials understands WHY there are two rows rather than following steps by rote.

activities.title: Consolidation: spot-the-error and estimate checks
feedback: For the spot-the-error item: the second row is ×20, so it must occupy the tens — the 0 marks the empty ones place, meaning '×20 not ×2'.
For the estimate item: rounding 48 to 50 and 52 to 50 gives 2,500, close to the true product 2,496, so it is a good magnitude check.
activities.rationale: Procedural consolidation with error-spotting and estimation tests and reinforces the procedure efficiently. This recognition/fill-in format checks the procedure rather than independently eliciting construction of the area link, so it is best used after the construction activities, not in place of them.
learnerActions: Examine a worked 34 × 27 in which the placeholder zero is missing from the second partial product; identify the error and explain why the zero belongs there.
Fill in a missing second partial product in a given long-multiplication layout.
Choose or state the best estimate for 48 × 52 by rounding both factors (≈ 50 × 50 = 2,500).
activities.intendedInsight: The missing placeholder zero and estimation are the quickest self-checks for magnitude; recognising the error reinforces the place-value reasoning behind the shifted row.

constraints: Recognition and fill-in/spot-the-error tasks consolidate the procedure but do not elicit the child independently constructing an area model and mapping it to the written method; use them after, not instead of, the bridging construction work.

Annotated static worked examples (area model above, written method below, tap to reveal each partial product's region) are useful reference scaffolds, but a fixed example cannot give feedback on a child's own fresh calculation or their own placeholder-zero error — pair them with tasks the child computes.

Spoken dialogue alone lacks a shared visible written layout, so it cannot display aligned columns or reliably catch column-placement errors in this spatial, multi-step procedure; keep a written/drawn layout at the centre rather than relying on talk alone (this is a layout-affordance limit, not a claim that dialogue can never support the procedure).

The area model is a conceptual scaffold for place value; the goal is eventual fluent compact long multiplication with the area link available for self-diagnosis, not permanent dependence on drawing grids.
Treat carrying/alignment slips as performance errors (re-estimate and recheck the flagged column) rather than reteaching the whole method.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic self-audit (all confirmed correct): 34×7=238, 34×20=680, 238+680=918; area tiles 600+210+80+28=918; 2,347×6=14,082; 45×23 regions 800+120+100+15=1,035 and partials 135+900=1,035; 48×52=2,496 with estimate 50×50=2,500. The source's correctAnswer states the 45×23 region sum as 1,035 — matches.

The source's 3D-interactive dismissal ('3D adds cost without insight') was removed as a catalog-fit judgement rather than an established pedagogical law; the planar area model is simply the natural representation for this place-value procedure, stated without claiming 3D could teach nothing.
CCSS 5.NBT.5/4.NBT.5 and the NCETM/IES area-model guidance are marked verified:false in the row; they are retained as cited but their evidence strength is not independently confirmed here.

The original prerequisite reteach IDs (mt_18fK9sQdIz, mt_AQo4u7O4sM) are catalog-internal and have been dropped from learner-facing guidance; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in the feedback.

For 2,347 × 6 both rounding choices (2,000 and 2,300) are underestimates, so the true answer exceeds them; feedback states this explicitly so the estimate is not mistaken for a bracket that must contain the answer.

The Y5 curriculum claim attached to the 2,347×6 activity directly supports the content requirement the activity enacts; the progression/sequencing point stated in that rationale is an editorial judgement the claim does not itself assert.

probeDeeper: Why did you write a zero before the second row of the multiplication?
In your grid, which region equals 40 × 20, and how much is it?
How does adding the four grid regions match adding your two partial products?
assess.correctAnswer: 34 × 27 = 918 (34×7 = 238, 34×20 = 680, sum 918). 2,347 × 6 = 14,082. Area model for 45×23 has four regions 40×20=800, 40×3=120, 5×20=100, 5×3=15, sum 1035. The teacher watches for the placeholder zero when multiplying by the tens digit, correct partial products, and the child mapping each grid region to a partial product.

errorPatterns.pattern: omits the placeholder zero — multiplies by the tens digit as if it were ones (34×2 recorded as 68, not 680)
errorPatterns.nextMove: connect to the area model: the 34×20 region is twenty rows, worth 680, not 68; write the zero first to reserve the ones place, saying 'we are multiplying by twenty'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: second partial product is ten times too small; final total far too low

errorPatterns.pattern: treats 34×27 as 34×2 + 34×7 (adds tens and ones digits without place value), or only multiplies by one digit
errorPatterns.nextMove: draw all four regions of the grid so every part of 27 (20 and 7) multiplies every part of 34; nothing may be left out.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: partial products do not account for the full value of each digit; area model has missing regions

errorPatterns.pattern: carrying error within a partial product or misaligned column addition
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach the method; have the child estimate first and recheck the flagged column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: one partial product or the final addition wrong; often caught by estimate (34×27 ≈ 30×30 = 900)

responseLevels.gap: omits the placeholder zero, multiplies by only one digit, or cannot link the method to the area model.
responseLevels.full: executes long multiplication with correct placeholders and partial products, maps each partial to an area region, and checks against an estimate.
responseLevels.partial: completes 4-digit × 1-digit correctly but slips on the 2-digit × 2-digit placeholder, or draws the grid without connecting regions to partial products.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask the child to compute 34 × 27 by long multiplication while you watch, and separately to compute 2,347 × 6. Then ask them to draw an area (grid) model for 45 × 23 and point to where each partial product sits. Watch the placeholder zero on the tens row and whether the partial products match the area regions.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Long multiplication's signature failure is the missing placeholder zero on the second partial product (multiplying by 2 tens but recording as 2 ones). Connecting the written partials to the four area regions distinguishes a child who understands WHY there are partial products from one following steps by rote.
